planting.note: Broadcast scarified seed onto warm, sandy, low-fertility soil after the last frost; Wynn self-sows readily once established, so plan on it returning as a volunteer cover in subsequent summers.

directions: Broadcast seed at 2-4 lb/ac onto bare, warm, sandy soil and press in lightly; Wynn is an Australian-bred cultivar of this short-lived perennial legume selected for broader leaflets and heavier seed set than wild roundleaf cassia types. It thrives on the deep, infertile sandy soils common across the Gulf Coastal Plain where many other cover legumes struggle, fixing nitrogen and raising companion grass protein content without needing lime or heavy fertility inputs. Mow or graze before hard frost; in zone 8-9 it typically behaves as a reseeding annual, returning from dropped seed the following warm season rather than persisting as a true perennial.

planting.note: Drill or broadcast into a firm, warm seedbed after danger of frost; German Strain R matures fast enough to serve as a short-window summer cover between a spring and fall vegetable planting.

directions: Drill 15-20 lb/ac (or broadcast 20-30 lb/ac) a quarter to a half inch deep into a firm, warm seedbed; German Strain R is a fine-stemmed, early-maturing foxtail millet selection valued for quick, leafy hay and quail/dove food-plot plantings across the Gulf South. Its compact seed heads and reddish-purple awns mature in as little as 40-50 days, making it one of the fastest routes to a weed-smothering stand of residue when a cover crop needs to fill a short summer gap. It has good seedling vigor and drought tolerance but little regrowth after cutting or grazing, so plan a single mow-and-terminate pass rather than a hay-type rotational cutting schedule.

planting.note: Broadcast scarified, inoculated seed into well-drained soil once it is reliably warm; Aztec's trailing vines need several weeks of heat to cover ground fully, so plant well after frost risk has passed.

directions: Broadcast 4-6 lb/ac of scarified, rhizobium-inoculated seed into warm, well-drained soil in full sun; Aztec is a rust-resistant Australian release of siratro, bred to replace the original 'Siratro' cultivar once bean rust (Uromyces appendiculatus) became a persistent problem in warm, humid climates like the Gulf Coast. Its deep taproot and dense, sprawling vines tolerate heat and drought once established, smothering weeds while fixing nitrogen for a following crop. Mow or graze before heavy pod set to limit volunteer reseeding, since siratro can persist and spread beyond the planted area in consistently frost-free zones.
sources: Queensland Department of Agriculture and Fisheries

planting.note: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a well-prepared, fertile seedbed after the soil has warmed; Tinaroo is a twining vine that is slower to establish than bush-type summer legumes and benefits from a weed-free start.

directions: Broadcast 4-6 lb/ac of inoculated seed onto a fertile, well-drained seedbed in full sun; Tinaroo is a Kenyan-origin glycine cultivar released in Queensland in 1962 that remains the most widely sown of the glycine pasture legumes for warm, humid climates. Its twining vines climb companion grasses to form a dense nitrogen-fixing canopy, but seedlings establish slowly compared to cowpea or lablab, so keep competing weeds down for the first several weeks. It needs consistent summer moisture to perform well and is best suited to the wetter end of the Gulf Coast cover-cropping window rather than drought-prone sites.

planting.note: Scarify and inoculate seed before broadcasting into warm, well-drained soil; Belalto establishes slowly and does best planted well after the soil has warmed in a weed-suppressed bed.

directions: Scarify and inoculate seed before broadcasting 2-4 lb/ac into warm, well-drained, acid-tolerant soil in full sun; Belalto is a Costa Rican-origin centro cultivar released in Australia in 1971 and selected for better cool-season growth and leaf-spot tolerance than common centro. Its twining vines climb and smother companion grasses or weeds while fixing nitrogen, and the species persists for years in consistently warm climates, so treat it as a longer-season ground cover rather than a quick single-summer fill. On the Gulf Coast it is best used where a planting can be left down for an extended period, since it is slow to establish and does not pay off its establishment cost in a single short rotation.

planting.note: Broadcast inoculated seed onto sandy, acidic, low-fertility soil after the soil warms; Oxley tolerates cooler nights better than most tropical stylos, which suits it to subtropical Gulf Coast summers.

directions: Broadcast 2-4 lb/ac of inoculated seed onto sandy, acidic, infertile soil in full sun; Oxley is a 1969 Australian release bred specifically for the subtropics, combining two stylo lines to improve seed-set timing over the wild composite population. Its fine, short stems and dense, low growth tolerate heavier grazing or mowing pressure than taller stylo types, and it holds up on the deep sandy soils typical of the Gulf Coastal Plain where fertility-demanding legumes fail. Mow or graze periodically to keep stands productive, and expect it to persist for several seasons as a reseeding perennial rather than needing annual replanting.
sources: ACIAR — Anthracnose Resistant Stylosanthes for Agricultural Systems

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto a well-prepared seedbed once soil is consistently warm; Katambora is a fine-leaved diploid type that establishes and sets seed faster than coarser tetraploid Rhodes grass cultivars.

directions: Broadcast 2-4 lb/ac onto a firm, warm seedbed and rake in lightly; Katambora is a Zimbabwe-origin diploid Rhodes grass cultivar originally selected for root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne spp.) suppression in tobacco rotations, a trait that also makes it a useful summer cover ahead of nematode-sensitive vegetable crops on the Gulf Coast. It tillers heavily, produces reliable seed, and tolerates alkaline or mildly saline soils better than most warm-season grasses. Mow or disk in before seed set if volunteer spread is a concern, since Rhodes grass can naturalize readily in consistently warm, humid regions.
